q: What are the Seneca I's sources of electrical power?
a: Two 60-amp alternators and a 12-volt, 35 amp-hour battery
d: Two 70-amp alternators and a 24-volt, 17 amp-hour battery
One 60-amp alternator on the left engine and a 12-volt, 35 amp-hour battery
Two 60-amp generators and a 24-volt, 35 amp-hour battery
why: Each engine drives its own 60-ampere alternator. The 12-volt, 35 Ah battery handles starting, power with engines off, and backup for the alternators.

q: To what voltage do the Seneca I's voltage regulators hold the electrical bus?
a: 14.0 volts
d: 12.0 volts
28.0 volts
24.0 volts
why: Two solid-state regulators keep the bus at 14.0 volts. It is a 14-volt system with a 12-volt battery, not a 28-volt system.

q: Where is the Seneca I's battery located?
a: In the nose, just forward of the nose baggage compartment
d: In the aft fuselage, behind the rear baggage compartment bulkhead
In the left engine nacelle, just aft of the engine firewall
Under the cockpit floor, beneath the front seats
why: The 12-volt battery sits in the nose section just forward of the nose baggage compartment and is reached through that compartment.

q: Per the POH, how should a run-down Seneca battery be recharged?
a: Remove it from the airplane; start at 4 amps and finish at 2 amps
d: Leave it installed and quick-charge it from a ground power cart
Leave it installed and charge at 10 amps with the master ON
Run both engines at 2000 RPM until the ammeters read zero
why: Section 2 says to remove the battery from the airplane to charge it. Section 9 gives the rate: start at 4 A, finish at 2 A. Quick charges are not recommended.

q: Your school's nose preflight checks the external power plug. Where on the Seneca is that receptacle?
a: Lower left side of the nose
d: Lower right side of the nose
Left side of the aft fuselage
Inside the nose baggage compartment
why: POH 2-12 and 9-8 put the external power receptacle on the lower left side of the nose. It is optional on the Seneca I, but your school preflight checks it. It takes a 12–14 volt source; keep the master OFF while plugging in or unplugging.

q: You are starting with Piper External Power (PEP). Where should the master switch be when plugging in, and during the start?
a: OFF while plugging in; ON for cranking and the start
d: ON while plugging in; OFF for cranking and the start
OFF for both, so the external source powers the starter
ON for both, so the battery assists the external source
why: Keep the master OFF while inserting or removing the plug to prevent sparking. Then turn it ON and do a normal start. The external source is a 12-volt battery (12–14 V).

q: After a start on external power, the POH has you remove the plug, turn the master back ON, and check what before flight?
a: Alternator output on the ammeter; don't fly if there is none
d: The voltmeter shows at least 12 volts on the battery
Both overvoltage lights come on when pressed
Both ammeters read zero with all equipment off
why: An external-power start usually means a weak battery. The POH says not to attempt flight unless the ammeter shows the alternator is producing output.

q: What does each alternator's overvoltage relay do?
a: Takes its alternator off line if its output voltage runs too high
d: Disconnects the battery from the bus if bus voltage drops too low
Limits that alternator's output current to its 60-amp rating
Opens the master solenoid to shed every electrical load at once
why: Some regulator failures let alternator voltage climb with nothing to stop it. The relay shuts that alternator off to protect the electrical and avionics equipment, and the red light shows the trip.

q: In cruise the left ammeter drops to zero, but the left OVERVOLTAGE light stays out. What does this mean?
a: The left alternator isn't producing current; the light shows only relay trips
d: The left alternator is fine, because any alternator failure would light that lamp
The left ammeter has failed, because the overvoltage light did not come on
The battery has taken over and the alternator will recover itself
why: A zero reading means that alternator is producing no current. The POH says the red light's only job is to show a tripped overvoltage relay; it may not come on for other alternator failures.

q: What do the Seneca I's two ammeters show?
a: Each alternator's output current, working as a load meter
d: Battery charge or discharge, on a center-zero scale
Bus voltage on each side of a split electrical bus
Current drawn by the avionics bus and the lighting bus
why: There is one ammeter per alternator, and each shows how much current its alternator is producing. Zero means that alternator is producing nothing. A reading near 60 means it is heavily loaded.

q: One ammeter is reading near 60 amps in cruise. What does the POH recommend?
a: Turn off unneeded equipment, since that alternator is being taxed
d: Nothing; about 60 amps is the normal cruise reading
Turn that alternator off and let the other one carry the whole load
Increase that engine's RPM so the alternator can produce more
why: A reading near 60 means demand is taxing that alternator, so reduce the load. The alternators already give rated output at low RPM, so adding RPM does not help.

q: Per the POH, what load should each alternator be limited to in flight, and why?
a: 50 amps, so some current is left to keep the battery charged
d: 60 amps, which is each alternator's full rated output
40 amps, to keep the alternators from overheating
35 amps, to match the battery's 35 amp-hour rating
why: The alternators can give 60 A, but Section 6 says to keep each at 50 A in flight so some current is always left to charge the battery. The emergency procedures also use the 50 A figure.

q: On one engine, why must you watch the electrical load on the remaining alternator?
a: An overloaded alternator may burn out or trip its circuit breaker
d: The good alternator's output is cut in half at single-engine power
The overvoltage relay trips whenever only one alternator is on line
The battery is disconnected from the bus when a prop is feathered
why: On one engine, one alternator carries everything. The POH warns that overloading it can burn it out or trip its breaker. Reduce the load to 50 A or less after an engine failure.

q: Engines running, all equipment off except the master, and the two ammeter readings add up to a significant amount. What does that suggest?
a: The battery has a low state of charge
d: An overvoltage relay is about to trip
One alternator is not sharing the load
A circuit breaker has tripped somewhere
why: With no loads on, the ammeters show only battery charging current plus instrument draw. A large total means the battery is taking a lot of charge. Find out why, or have a mechanic check the battery and system.

q: Where are the Seneca I's circuit breakers?
a: Lower right side of the instrument panel
d: On the switch panel to the left of the pilot
On the lower left panel beside the throttles
On the console between the two front seats
why: All circuit breakers are grouped in the lower right corner of the instrument panel, with room for more if equipment is added.
drop_reason: duplicate of p2-127 (circuit breakers grouped in the lower right of the panel; p2-127 also covers how to reset)

q: A circuit breaker trips. Per the POH, how should you reset it?
a: Allow two to five minutes to cool, then push it back in
d: Push it in right away and hold it in for five seconds
Pull it fully out, wait 30 seconds, then push it in
Cycle the master switch OFF and ON to reset it
why: A breaker trips on a malfunction or current surge. The Operating Tips say to let it cool two to five minutes, then push it in to reset.

q: Where are the master, magneto, fuel pump, starter, alternator, light and pitot heat switches?
a: On the switch panel to the left of the pilot
d: On the lower right panel above the circuit breakers
On an overhead panel above the windshield
On the pedestal below the power quadrant
why: Most electrical switches, including the master and the magnetos, are on the switch panel to the pilot's left. The red overvoltage lights are there too.

q: How do you test an overvoltage light in the Seneca I?
a: Turn that alternator switch OFF, then press the light
d: Press the light with that alternator switch ON
Turn the master OFF, then press both lights together
Pull that alternator's breaker and watch for the light
why: The press-to-test works only with that alternator switch OFF. A placard below the switches says so: "ALTERNATOR SWITCH OFF FOR OVER-VOLTAGE LAMP TEST."

q: What alternator check does the POH call for before flight?
a: Overvoltage lights work, and both ammeters about equal at 1500 RPM or more
d: Each ammeter shows exactly 60 amps with both engines at 2000 RPM
Both ammeters stay at zero until the engines reach 2000 RPM
Left ammeter about double the right with the engines at 1000 RPM
why: Check that the overvoltage lights work, and that both alternators show about the same output with both engines at 1500 RPM or above.

q: Both OVERVOLTAGE lights come on. You shed all loads except the master and turn both alternator switches OFF. What next?
a: Briefly turn each ON, watching the ammeters; leave the one with LEAST output ON
d: Leave both OFF and land as soon as possible on battery power alone
Turn both back ON together, then cycle the master switch OFF and ON
Briefly turn each ON, watching the ammeters; leave the one with MOST output ON
why: Turn each alternator on briefly, one at a time, and leave on the one with the least output. Keep the load under 50 A. If both show about equal output under 50 A, turn both on and resume normal operation.

q: After lots of restart cranking the battery is weak, and the good alternator has dropped off line. What may bring it back, per the POH?
a: Shed heavy loads, operating alternator ON, master OFF briefly, then master ON
d: Leave the master ON and cycle the operating alternator switch several times
Leave the master ON and turn both alternator switches OFF, then ON
Turn the master OFF for the rest of the flight to save the battery
why: First check the alternator breakers. Shed heavy loads with their own switches, not the master. Then turn the master off for a short time and back on, and watch the ammeter. If there's no output, repeat with longer waits.

q: An alternator fails in icing conditions and can't be restored. What does the POH say to keep on, and what to turn off?
a: Keep one NAVCOM and transponder; turn off the electric windshield
d: Keep windshield and pitot heat; turn off the transponder
Keep prop deice and all radios; turn off pitot heat
Keep everything on and let the battery cover the shortfall
why: This keeps the load within 60 A. Leave icing as soon as practical. The windshield heat may be turned back on before landing, but the battery may be depleted and the gear may need free-fall extension.

q: What starter limits does the POH give?
a: Crank for no more than 30 seconds, then let it cool several minutes
d: Crank for no more than 10 seconds, then let it cool one minute
Crank for no more than 60 seconds, then let it cool 30 seconds
No limit applies, as long as oil pressure is rising
why: To protect the starter, crank for no more than 30 seconds at a time, then wait several minutes. Don't re-engage the starter right after releasing it.

q: Why does the POH want radio, light and pitot heat switches off before engine start?
a: So the system isn't overloaded when the starter engages
d: So the overvoltage relays don't trip during the start
So the master solenoid contacts don't weld closed
Because the alternators can't carry any load at idle
why: The starter is the biggest single electrical load. Turning other loads off first avoids an overloaded condition when it is engaged.

q: If the master switch is turned OFF with both engines running, what happens?
a: The engines keep running; magneto ignition doesn't need ship's power
d: Both engines quit, because the ignition runs off the main bus
The engines keep running only if the electric fuel pumps are on
The left engine quits, and the right runs on its own alternator
why: Ignition comes from the engine-driven magnetos, and fuel comes from engine-driven pumps. The external-power start procedure itself has you turn the master off with the engine running.

q: Which Seneca I flight instruments are vacuum-driven?
a: The attitude indicators and directional gyros
d: The attitude indicators and turn indicators
The directional gyros and airspeed indicators
The attitude indicators, directional gyros and turn indicators
why: The vacuum system draws filtered cabin air through the attitude and heading gyros. The turn indicator is electric, which is why the POH uses it as a cross-check when vacuum fails.

q: How is vacuum supplied in the Seneca I?
a: An engine-driven vacuum pump on each engine
d: A single electric vacuum pump in the nose
One engine-driven pump on the left engine only
Venturi tubes on each side of the fuselage
why: There is one pump on each engine, plus plumbing, regulators, filters, and a check valve. Either pump alone can run the gyros.

q: What vacuum do the Seneca's regulators maintain, and at what RPM?
a: 5.0 ±0.1 in. Hg at 2000 RPM
d: 4.5 ±0.1 in. Hg at 1500 RPM
5.2 ±0.1 in. Hg at 2700 RPM
5.0 ±0.5 in. Hg at idle RPM
why: A regulator on the right aft side of each firewall holds 5.0 ±0.1 in. Hg at 2000 RPM. The Operating Tips list what to check before flight if the gauge doesn't show this.

q: What are the Seneca I's vacuum gauge operating limits?
a: 4.5 to 5.2 in. Hg
d: 4.0 to 5.0 in. Hg
4.8 to 5.5 in. Hg
3.5 to 4.5 in. Hg
why: The Limitations section gives 4.5 to 5.2 in. Hg for all operations. Below 4.5, airflow through the gyros is low and their readings may be wrong.

q: What does a vacuum reading below 4.5 in. Hg indicate?
a: Low airflow through the gyros, so their readings may be inaccurate
d: Normal operation; the gauge reads this low in every phase of flight
Too much suction, which may overspeed and damage the gyros
Normal single-pump operation, as long as one red button shows
why: Below 4.5 in. Hg, not enough air is moving through the gyro instruments to keep them accurate. Low readings are expected only at low RPM or very high altitude.

q: The left engine fails and is feathered. What must you do to keep the gyros powered?
a: Nothing; a check valve automatically isolates the failed side
d: Select the right pump with the vacuum selector valve on the panel
Turn on the standby electric vacuum pump with its own switch
Open the alternate air to restore suction
why: When one pump or one side's hose loses suction, the check valve closes by itself and the other pump supplies vacuum. The red button for that side shows on the gauge. No pilot selection is needed.

q: How does the Seneca's vacuum gauge show that one side has lost suction?
a: A red malfunction button appears for that side
d: The needle moves into a red arc for that side
An amber VACUUM light comes on in the annunciator panel
The needle drops to zero and stays there
why: The gauge has two red buttons, one per side. A button shows when that side's pump has failed or its engine is feathered.

q: On one engine, up to what altitude can a single vacuum pump run a dual set of gyros?
a: 12,500 ft; above that, keep a high RPM
d: 10,000 ft; above that, you must descend
15,000 ft; above that, open alternate air
Any altitude, if RPM is at least 2000
why: Each pump alone can drive both sets of gyros up to 12,500 ft. Above that, a high RPM is needed on the remaining pump to keep enough suction.

q: Vacuum drops below 4.5 in. Hg in flight. What does the POH tell you to do?
a: Go to 2700 RPM, descend if able, and cross-check with the electric turn indicator
d: Feather the engine with the failed pump and continue at cruise power
Reduce RPM to 2000, climb, and cross-check with the electric turn indicator
Pull and reset the vacuum circuit breaker, then recheck the gauge
why: More RPM gives more suction, and descending helps keep 4.5 in. Hg. Use the electric turn indicator to judge whether the attitude and heading gyros can still be trusted.

q: Per the Operating Tips, which of these is a normal cause of a low vacuum reading, not a malfunction?
a: Low engine RPM, such as on approach or in training maneuvers
d: A dirty or restricted common air filter behind the panel
A collapsed or broken vacuum line behind the panel
Worn vacuum pumps that no longer pull full suction
why: A low reading is normal at low RPM and at very high altitude (above 12,000 ft). The dirty filter, damaged lines and worn pumps are items to check before flight.

q: Where is the Seneca I's pitot source, and which instrument uses it?
a: Aluminum mast under the left wing; airspeed indicator only
d: Mast under the right wing; airspeed indicator and altimeter
Probe on the nose; airspeed indicator only
Mast under the left wing; airspeed indicator and VSI
why: Pitot (total) pressure comes from the mast under the left wing. It feeds only the airspeed indicator.

q: Where are the Seneca I's static sources?
a: One on each side of the rear fuselage, connected inside
d: A single flush port on the left side of the rear fuselage
Built into the pitot mast under the left wing, aft of the inlet
One on each side of the nose, just below the windshield
why: Two static units, one on each side of the aft fuselage, are tied together inside. A slip or skid raises pressure on one side and lowers it on the other, and the connection averages them out.

q: Which Seneca I instruments use static pressure?
a: Altimeter, vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator
d: Altimeter and vertical speed indicator only
Altimeter, vertical speed indicator and the attitude indicator
Airspeed indicator and the manifold pressure gauges
why: The altimeter, VSI and airspeed indicator all use static pressure. The airspeed indicator also gets pitot pressure.

q: What ice protection does your Seneca's pitot-static system have?
a: A heated pitot mast; the static ports are not heated
d: A heated pitot and heated static ports
Heated static ports only; the pitot is not heated
None at all; the alternate static is the only backup
why: The pitot mast has a heating element for ice or heavy rain (an option on the Seneca I; your school preflight checks it warm). The static sensors are not heated, because experience shows they are unlikely to ice up.

q: Where is the alternate static source control, and what static source does it use?
a: Below the panel, right of the power quadrant; cabin air pressure
d: Below the panel, left of the pilot; outside air from the tailcone
On the left switch panel; cabin air pressure
Right of the power quadrant; air from the pitot mast
why: With the valve in the alternate position, the altimeter, VSI and airspeed indicator take static pressure from the cabin, so their readings may change slightly.

q: With alternate static selected, what does the POH say can change your instrument readings?
a: Airspeed, heater and vent settings, and the storm window
d: Only airspeed; the heater and vent settings have no effect
Outside air temperature, humidity and the altimeter setting
Pitot heat and the load on the alternators
why: These all change cabin pressure. You can see the effect by switching sources at different speeds and vent settings, including the storm window open, which is allowed only below 150 MPH.

q: You suspect water in the static system. Per the POH, how do you drain it?
a: Select alternate static; its valve is at the system's low point
d: Open the drain valve in the lower left front side panel
Turn on pitot heat long enough to evaporate the water in the lines
Blow out the static ports with low-pressure shop air
why: The alternate static selector valve is at the lowest point of the static system, so selecting alternate drains it. The drain in the lower left side panel is for the pitot line. The walk-around says to drain both before flight.

q: What does the drain in the lower left front side panel remove moisture from?
a: The pitot line between the mast and the instrument panel
d: The static lines running from the rear fuselage static ports
The fuel crossfeed line running under the cabin floor
The vacuum system's common air filter
why: That drain is for the pitot pressure line. Moisture in the static system is drained by selecting the alternate static source.

q: What provides the cabin and defroster heat in your Seneca?
a: A heat exchanger (muff) on each engine's exhaust manifold
d: A Janitrol combustion heater mounted in the nose baggage area
Electric heating elements under the cabin floor panels
Air bled from the engine-driven vacuum pumps
why: Each engine has a heater muff around its exhaust manifold. That is your Seneca's only cabin heat; the optional Janitrol combustion heater (aft fuselage) is not installed.

q: Where does air for the exhaust heater muffs come in?
a: Through a scoop on the outboard side of each cowling
d: Through the inlets in each wing's leading edge
Through an inlet at the base of the vertical fin
Through a scoop on the inboard side of each nacelle
why: Air enters a scoop on the outboard side of each cowling and is heated in the muff. A heat-and-defrost valve on the firewall sends it to the windshield or the cabin.

q: Where does fresh air for the cabin and for the overhead outlets come from?
a: Wing leading-edge inlets; the overhead outlets are fed from inlets on the fin
d: Cowling scoops on each engine; the overhead outlets are fed from wing-root inlets
Nose inlets; the overhead outlets are fed from a roof scoop
Wing leading-edge inlets; the overhead outlets are fed from the heater muffs
why: Fresh air for the heat mixing box comes in through each wing's leading edge. The overhead outlets take air from inlets on each side of the lower leading edge of the vertical fin.

q: How does the standard heating system control cabin temperature?
a: A control box mixes muff-heated air with fresh air from the wing inlets
d: A thermostat cycles the exhaust muffs on and off as needed
The pilot varies how much exhaust gas is routed through the heater muffs
A control box mixes muff-heated air with warm air from the oil coolers
why: Heated air from the muffs goes to a temperature-fresh air control box, where it is mixed with fresh air from the wing leading-edge inlets before entering the cabin.

q: Where does heated or fresh air enter the cabin for the occupants?
a: An outlet near each occupant's feet, plus adjustable overhead outlets
d: Only through the windshield defroster outlets and the side wall air vents
Only through adjustable overhead outlets in the ceiling
Through outlets along each cabin side wall at window level only
why: Each occupant has a floor outlet near the feet for heated or fresh air, as selected on the panel. Overhead outlets give fresh air: turn the rim counterclockwise for more flow, clockwise for less.

q: Where are the standard cabin heat and defroster controls?
a: On the right side of the instrument panel
d: On the console between the two front seats
On the switch panel to the left of the pilot
On the pedestal below the power quadrant
why: The cabin heat and defroster controls for the standard muff system are on the right side of the instrument panel.

q: How is the defroster blower turned on and off?
a: Lever at full on/HI starts it; moving it back about an inch stops it
d: With a separate DEFROST BLOWER switch on the left switch panel
It runs whenever the master switch is ON and cannot be turned off
It runs whenever cabin heat is on and stops when heat is off
why: The blower defogs the windshield on the ground. It runs when the defrost lever is at full on/HI, and moving the lever back about an inch shuts it off in flight.

q: Per the POH, how do you get maximum windshield defrosting?
a: Turn cabin heat off and the defroster full on
d: Turn cabin heat and the defroster both full on
Turn the defroster on and open the storm window
Turn the defroster on and select alternate air
why: Shutting off cabin heat sends all available hot air to the windshield outlets.

q: Where is the optional Janitrol combustion heater installed?
a: In the aft fuselage
d: In the nose section
In the right engine nacelle
Under the floor between the front seats
why: The Janitrol heater is in the aft fuselage. It adds heat for the cabin and defrosting on top of the standard muff system.

q: What are the positions of the combustion heater's three-position switch, and what does FAN do?
a: FAN, OFF, HEATER; FAN runs only the ventilation blower
d: OFF, LOW, HIGH; LOW runs the blower with the burner at half
OFF, ON, DEFROST; DEFROST sends all heat to the windshield
FAN, HEATER, RESET; FAN runs the blower and burner together
why: The switch is on the console between the front seats. FAN is for ventilation or defogging on the ground when you don't want heat.

q: You select HEATER, but neither the combustion heater's fan nor its burner runs. What is the likely cause?
a: The air intake lever is still in the closed position
d: The right fuel selector is on CROSSFEED instead of ON
The standard defroster lever is not in the HI position
The right auxiliary fuel pump has not been turned on
why: Two safety switches at the intake valve block both fan and heater operation until the air intake lever is moved off the closed position. A fuel problem would stop the burner but not the fan.

q: Where does the combustion heater get its fuel, and how much does it burn?
a: Right engine's line between engine pump and injector; 1/2 gal/hr
d: Left engine's line just downstream of the gascolator; 1 gal/hr
Its own small fuel tank in the aft fuselage; 1/2 gal/hr
Right engine's line ahead of the fuel selector; 2 gal/hr
why: Include heater fuel in flight planning. With the right fuel selector OFF, the heater will not work. Fuel flow starts only when the switch is set to HEATER.

q: The right engine has failed and been secured. Can you still run the combustion heater?
a: Yes: right selector ON, right mixture idle cutoff, right aux pump ON
d: No; the heater stops working whenever the right engine is stopped
Yes, by putting the left fuel selector on CROSSFEED
Yes, but only on FAN, because no fuel can reach the burner
why: The heater draws from the right engine's fuel line. With the selector on and the mixture in idle cutoff, the aux pump can supply it. First make sure there are no fuel leaks between the tank and the engine.

q: Where does the combustion heater show an overheat, and where is the overheat switch's reset button?
a: Light on the heater console; reset button on the heater, via the aft bulkhead panel
d: Light on the annunciator panel; reset button on the face of the heater control console
Light on the heater console; reset button on the lower right circuit breaker panel
Light on the left switch panel; reset by cycling the heater switch to OFF
why: The heat-limit switch lights the overheat light on the console between the front seats. Its red reset button is on the heater shroud in the aft fuselage, reached through the bulkhead access panel. Don't restart the heater until the cause has been found and fixed.

q: The combustion heater overheat light comes on in flight. What does the POH say?
a: Don't restart it until it's inspected and the cause is fixed
d: Wait 15 seconds with the intake open, then select HEATER again
Press the red reset button on the console, then select HEATER
Run the fan for two minutes to cool it, then select HEATER
why: The red reset button is on the heater shroud in the aft fuselage, reached through a bulkhead access panel, not from the seat. The supplement says not to restart until the cause has been found and fixed.

q: What is the proper combustion heater shutdown on the ground?
a: Switch to FAN for two minutes with the intake open, then OFF
d: Switch to OFF, then close the air intake lever right away
Close the air intake lever, then run FAN for 15 seconds
Pull the heater circuit breaker, then switch to OFF
why: Running the fan with the intake open cools the heater so the overheat switch doesn't trip. In flight, leave the intake open at least 15 seconds after switching the heater OFF.

q: Per the combustion heater supplement, above what altitude is heater operation not approved?
why: The supplement does not approve heater operation above 20,000 ft. Its other limitation, no electric windshield heat at the same time because of compass error, is placarded near the heater controls.

q: When is a Seneca I approved for flight into known icing conditions?
a: Only with the complete optional Piper ice protection system installed
d: Whenever pitot heat and the heated windshield panel are both installed
Whenever the heated pitot and propeller deice both work
Never; no Seneca I can be approved for known icing
why: Known-icing approval requires the full system: boots, prop deice, electric windshield panel, heated pitot, heated stall warning transmitters, anti-icing fuel vents, governor shields and deflectors, and the wing ice light. Your Seneca has no ice protection system, so flight in icing is prohibited.

q: Which of these is on the POH's list of equipment required for flight into known icing?
a: Anti-icing fuel tank vents
d: Heated static ports
Engine air inlet lip heaters
An alcohol windshield spray system
why: The list includes anti-icing fuel vents (one under each wing) so ice can't block the tank vent lines. The static ports are not heated in the Seneca.

q: What holds the deice boots flat when the surface deice system is off?
a: Constant suction from the engine-driven vacuum pumps
d: Spring tension molded into the rubber boot material itself
Ram air pressure on the leading edges
A separate electric vacuum pump mounted in the tail cone
why: Suction from the engine-driven vacuum pumps keeps the boots smooth and streamlined between cycles, and it is reapplied after each inflation.

q: Where are the pneumatic deice boots on a Seneca with the ice protection system?
a: On the wing, vertical fin and stabilator leading edges
d: On the wing leading edges only; the tail is unprotected
On the wing and stabilator leading edges only
On the wings, fin, stabilator and the engine nacelle inlets
why: Boots cover the wing, vertical fin and horizontal stabilator leading edges. The props have electric deicer pads instead.

q: What happens when you press the momentary SURFACE DE-ICE switch once?
a: A timer inflates all boots for about six seconds, then they deflate
d: The boots stay inflated for as long as the switch is held
The boots cycle over and over until the switch is turned off
The wing boots inflate, then the tail boots six seconds later
why: The timer powers the pressure control valves for six seconds and the WING-TAIL DE-ICER light comes on. Then the air is dumped overboard and suction returns. Do not hold the switch ON.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: surface deice switch/boots

q: Per the POH, when should the pneumatic boots be cycled?
a: When 1/4 to 1/2 inch of ice has built up
d: Continuously, as soon as any ice is seen
Only after about 1 inch of ice has built up
Before entering icing, to keep the boots clear
why: Cycling with less than 1/4 inch can leave a cavity under the ice so it won't come off. Waiting past 1/2 inch may also leave ice the boots can't shed.

q: After you cycle the boots, the WING-TAIL DE-ICER light stays on for more than 20 seconds. What do you do?
a: Pull the surface deice circuit breaker
d: Press the SURFACE DE-ICE switch again
Turn the master switch OFF and back ON
Nothing; the light stays on until the ice sheds
why: A normal cycle lasts about six seconds. A light on for more than 20 seconds means the system is stuck, and the POH says to pull the surface deice breaker.

q: Where is the wing ice detection light?
a: On the outboard side of the left engine nacelle
d: On the inboard side of the left engine nacelle
In the left wingtip, shining inboard
Under the nose, shining aft at both wings
why: It lets you check the wing for ice during night flight. It has an ICE LIGHT switch to the right of the SURFACE DE-ICE switch and its own WING ICE LIGHT circuit breaker.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: wing ice light

q: How do the Seneca's electrothermal propeller deicers work?
a: Timer heats each pad's outboard, then inboard half, via slip rings
d: Pads heated all at once and continuously while the switch is on
Fluid pumped from a tank through slinger rings onto each blade
Hot governor oil circulated through the hub and blade roots
why: Each pad has an outboard and an inboard heater. Current goes from the timer through brush blocks to slip rings on the starter ring gear. Heating loosens the ice, and centrifugal force and the airstream throw it off in small pieces.

q: What is the propeller deice heating sequence?
a: Right outboard, right inboard, left outboard, left inboard
d: Left outboard, left inboard, right outboard, right inboard
Right inboard, right outboard, left inboard, left outboard
Both outboard halves together, then both inboard halves
why: The cycle may start at any step, depending on where the timer stopped last time. It then runs in this order until the system is turned off.

q: How is the propeller deice checked during preflight?
a: Turn PROP DE-ICE on and feel the pads warm in the proper sequence
d: Turn it on and watch the ammeter only; don't touch the pads
Run the engines at 2000 RPM and watch for the pads to steam
Press the test button and listen for the timer to click
why: The POH preflight is a touch check. The pads should get warm in the timer's order. Section 6 suggests 30 seconds for the heat checks.

q: What limits ground operation of the heated windshield panel?
a: No more than 30 seconds, unless in flight or ice is on the panel
d: No more than 2 minutes, and only with at least one engine running
It may not be turned on at all on the ground
No more than 60 seconds, and only with both alternators on line
why: The supplement says never run it more than 30 seconds unless the airplane is flying or there is ice on the panel. Operation is checked by feeling the glass warm.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: heated windshield panel

q: What extra document does the windshield heating installation require?
a: A second compass deviation card, with windshield heat and radios on
d: A separate weight and balance record for the heated panel
A maintenance logbook entry before every flight into icing conditions
A placard limiting airspeed while the windshield heat is on
why: The heated windshield affects the magnetic compass, so a second deviation card is required. For the same reason, it can't be used at the same time as the combustion heater.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: heated windshield panel

q: Which switch heats the stall warning lift detectors?
a: The HEATED PITOT switch
d: A separate STALL WARN HEAT switch
The SURFACE DE-ICE switch
The windshield panel heat switch
why: One ON-OFF HEATED PITOT switch on the left switch panel heats the pitot head and both left-wing lift detectors. They have separate PITOT HEAT and STALL WARN HEAT breakers, and both get very hot during the check.

q: What do the propeller governor ice shields and deflectors do?
a: Keep ice entering the front cowl opening off the governor
d: Throw ice shed by the spinner clear of the cowling openings
Warm the governor oil so the prop responds normally in icing
Turn ice thrown off the props away from the cabin windows
why: They stop ice and other particles that come in through the front cowl opening from interfering with governor operation.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: propeller governor ice shields are part of the ice protection system

q: On entering icing conditions, which items does the POH say to turn on immediately?
a: Pitot heat, windshield heat and prop deice
d: Pitot heat, windshield heat and the wing boots
Wing boots, prop deice and the ice light
Prop deice and the wing boots only
why: The defroster goes on before entering icing. The wing boots wait until 1/4 to 1/2 inch of ice builds up. If the props vibrate from uneven ice, briefly increase RPM.

q: In prolonged icing, how much may the Seneca's stall speed increase, per the POH?
a: Up to 12 mph
d: Up to 5 mph
Up to 20 mph
Up to 30 mph
why: With ice on unprotected surfaces, buffet starts 5 to 10 mph above the stall. Stall speed may rise by up to 12 mph, so keep a good margin above normal stall speeds.

q: What performance penalty does the POH give for installing the ice protection equipment?
a: 30 fpm less single-engine climb; 850 ft lower single-engine ceiling
d: 50 fpm less single-engine climb; 500 ft lower single-engine ceiling
No change; the supplements say performance is unchanged
100 fpm less two-engine climb; 1,500 ft lower service ceiling
why: The Flight in Known Icing section notes the installation costs 30 fpm of single-engine climb and 850 ft of single-engine service ceiling.

q: Does the Seneca I have protection against induction air icing?
a: Yes: manual alternate air, heated by the crossover exhaust tube
d: Yes: alternate air doors that open by themselves if the filter clogs
Yes: a carburetor heat control for each engine
No: fuel injection makes induction icing impossible
why: Alternate air is controlled by the pilot, not automatically. It is heated and bypasses the filter, so it protects against snow or freezing rain blocking the filter. Apply it early, and avoid it for ground operation (unfiltered air).

q: How does the Seneca I warn of an approaching stall?
a: A light and horn, triggered by two lift detectors on the left wing
d: A horn only, triggered by a single vane on the right wing
A stick shaker, triggered by an angle-of-attack vane on the nose
A light only, triggered by a pressure port in the left wing
why: Two lift detectors sit on the leading edge of the left wing, outboard of the nacelle. Heated detectors are part of the optional ice protection system.

q: Which lift detector activates the stall warning with the flaps at 25° or 40°?
a: The inboard detector
d: The outboard detector
Both detectors together
Neither; the warning is disabled at 40°
why: The inboard detector works with the flaps at 25° and 40°. The outboard one works at the other settings (0° and 10°).

q: On preflight, with the flaps fully down, you lift the outboard stall vane and the horn stays silent. Is the system faulty?
a: Not necessarily; the outboard vane works only with flaps at 0° or 10°
d: Yes; either vane should sound the horn at any flap setting from 0° to 40°
Yes; the outboard vane is the one that works at 40°
Not necessarily; the horn works only with an engine running
why: With flaps at 25° or 40°, only the inboard detector is active. The school preflight tests the outboard vane at 0–10° and the inboard vane at 25–40°, which matches the POH.

q: How can you tell the stall warning horn from the gear warning horn?
a: The two horns have different sounds
d: They sound the same; check which light is on
The stall horn sounds only with the flaps down
The gear warning has no horn, only a red light
why: The POH says the stall warning horn sounds different from the landing gear warning horn. The stall warning also has its own light.

q: When towing the Seneca I with power equipment, what is the nose gear turn limit?
a: 20° either side of center
d: 30° either side of center
42° either side of center
45° either side of center
why: Turning the nose gear more than 20° either way while power-towing damages the nose gear and steering mechanism. Don't confuse this with the 42° total arc the rudder pedals steer.

q: What are the Seneca I's tire pressures?
a: Nose 31 psi; mains 53 psi
d: Nose 53 psi; mains 31 psi
Nose 35 psi; mains 50 psi
Nose 31 psi; mains 42 psi
why: Keep the nose tire at 31 psi and the mains at 53 psi for best tire life. The POH also suggests swapping tires periodically so they wear evenly.

q: How much oleo strut should be exposed with the airplane at rest (static load)?
a: Mains 3-1/2 inches; nose 2-1/2 inches
d: Mains 2-1/2 inches; nose 3-1/2 inches
Mains 4-1/2 inches; nose 3-1/2 inches
All three struts 3 inches
why: Sections 9 and 6 both give 3-1/2 in. for the main struts and 2-1/2 in. for the nose. The school preflight checklist uses the same figures.

q: What hydraulic fluid goes in the Seneca I brake system?
a: MIL-H-5606 (petroleum base)
d: MIL-H-83282 (synthetic base)
Skydrol (phosphate ester base)
DOT 3 brake fluid (glycol base)
why: The POH specifies MIL-H-5606 petroleum-base fluid. The lubrication chart also warns against hydraulic fluid with a castor oil or ester base.

q: Where is the brake fluid reservoir, and when should it be checked?
a: Top rear of the nose baggage area; periodically and each 100-hour
d: Behind the left main gear; at each annual inspection only
Built into the gear hydraulic power pack; at every 50-hour inspection
Under the pilot's floor panel; checked as part of every preflight
why: It's behind a panel marked "Brake Reservoir Behind" at the top rear of the nose baggage compartment. Keep the fluid at the marked level; your school's nose preflight also checks it. The gear system has its own separate reservoir built into the gear pump.

q: Where are the jack points for servicing?
a: One outboard of each main gear and one just aft of the nose gear
d: One inboard of each main gear and one under the tail skid
One under each wingtip and one at the tail tie-down
One at each main gear axle and one at the nose gear axle
why: There are three jack points: one outboard of each main gear and one just aft of the nose gear. The airplane goes on jacks to check the gear after an emergency extension for a malfunction.

q: How does the POH say to tie down the Seneca?
a: Ropes to the wing rings and tail skid at about 45°, using bowline knots
d: Ropes straight down from the wing rings and tail skid, using slip knots
Ropes to the propeller hubs and nose gear fork, using bowlines
Chains around both main gear struts only, pulled tight at 90° to the ground
why: Head into the wind if possible, lock the controls with the wheel lock or surface blocks, block the wheels, then tie down at about 45°. Use bowlines, never slip knots, and install the pitot cover.

q: Per the POH ground handling section, how should the propellers be set for taxiing?
a: Low pitch, high RPM
d: High pitch, low RPM
Midrange pitch, to cut prop noise
Feathered on whichever engine isn't needed
why: Taxi with the props in low pitch, high RPM. Avoid high RPM over loose stones or gravel, which can damage the blades.

q: What are the Seneca I engines' oil capacity and minimum safe quantity?
a: 8 quarts capacity; 2 quarts minimum safe
d: 8 quarts capacity; 6 quarts minimum safe
6 quarts capacity; 2 quarts minimum safe
12 quarts capacity; 6 quarts minimum safe
why: Each Lycoming holds 8 quarts, and 2 quarts is the minimum safe quantity. The walk-around asks you to see six to eight quarts before flight.

q: Ambient temperatures are expected to be about 95°F. Which oil grade does the POH require?
a: SAE 50
d: SAE 40
SAE 30
SAE 20
why: The POH table: SAE 50 above 60°F, SAE 40 from 30–90°F, SAE 30 from 0–70°F, and SAE 20 below 10°F. Only the SAE 50 range covers 95°F.

q: Ambient temperatures are expected to be about 20°F. Which oil grade does the POH require?
a: SAE 30
d: SAE 40
SAE 50
SAE 20
why: 20°F falls only in the SAE 30 range (0–70°F). SAE 40 starts at 30°F and SAE 20 is for below 10°F.

q: How often does the POH recommend oil changes, and when may the interval be extended?
a: Every 50 hr; up to double with a full-flow filter changed each 50 hr
d: Every 100 hr; up to 50% longer with any type of oil filter or screen
Every 25 hr; up to double with a screen-type oil filter
Every 50 hours; no extension is allowed under any condition
why: Drain and refill every 50 hours, or sooner in bad conditions. With full-flow cartridge filters, the interval can be up to doubled, as long as the filter element is replaced every 50 hours.

q: How often must the induction air filters be cleaned, and when must they be replaced?
a: Clean at least every 50 hours; replace after 1 year or 500 hours
d: Clean every 100 hours; replace after 2 years or 1,000 hours
Clean every 25 hours; replace after 1 year or 250 hours
Clean every 50 hours; replace only when the element is torn
why: Clean them at least every 50 hours, more often in dusty conditions. Tap them clean (no compressed air or solvents), and replace if torn or after 1 year or 500 hours, whichever comes first.

q: What gas does the POH recommend for charging the propeller dome?
a: Dry nitrogen
d: Carbon dioxide
Argon
Oxygen
why: Dry nitrogen is recommended. Section 2 allows compressed air only if it has no moisture, since moisture may freeze the piston in cold weather.

q: How does the propeller dome pressure change with temperature, per the POH?
a: It rises about 1/3 psi for each 1°F increase
d: It rises about 1 psi for each 1°F increase
It rises about 1/10 psi for each 1°F increase
It stays fixed; temperature has no effect
why: The Section 9 text gives about 1/3 psi per °F, so allow for temperature and charge to the spinner-cap placard. (The POH's chamber pressure table itself steps about 2 psi per 10°F.)

q: Per the POH chamber pressure table, what prop dome charge is required at 70°F?
a: 80 psi
d: 72 psi
86 psi
66 psi
why: From the table: 70°F needs 80 psi. 30°F needs 72 psi, 100°F needs 86 psi, and 0°F needs 66 psi.

q: What does the POH say not to do when checking or charging the propeller dome?
a: Don't check or charge it with the propeller feathered
d: Don't check it when the engine and propeller are cold
Don't charge it with dry nitrogen
Don't check it against the placard in the spinner cap
why: The note under the chamber pressure table says never to check or charge the pressure with the propeller feathered.

q: What is the minimum fuel grade for the Seneca I, per the POH?
a: 100/130 octane aviation fuel
d: 80/87 octane aviation fuel
91/96 octane aviation fuel
Premium automotive gasoline
why: The POH requires at least 100/130 octane aviation grade. Lower grades can cause serious engine damage quickly and void the engine warranty.

q: Per Section 9, how much fuel does each wing hold when filled to the bottom of the filler neck?
a: 49 gallons per side, 98 gallons total
d: 47 gallons per side, 94 gallons total
45 gallons per side, 90 gallons total
50 gallons per side, 100 gallons total
why: Each wing holds up to 49 gallons, 98 gallons in all, when filled to the bottom of the filler neck with 100/130 fuel. Usable fuel is a Section 3 figure.

q: How often do the fuel strainer screens need cleaning?
a: Every 50 hours or 90 days, whichever comes first
d: Every 100 hours or 12 months, whichever comes first
Every 25 hours or 30 days, whichever comes first
Only at each annual inspection
why: The gascolator strainer screens are cleaned every 50 hours or 90 days, whichever comes first. The screen at the fuel injector inlet is cleaned every 50 hours.

q: Where are the fuel gascolator strainers?
a: In the nacelles, between the fuel selector valves and the aux pumps
d: In the wings, between the tanks and the fuel selector valves
On the engines, between the engine pumps and the injectors
In the fuselage, at the low point of the crossfeed line
why: Each gascolator sits in its nacelle between the selector valve and the auxiliary boost pump. Its quick drain is near the bottom of the nacelle.

q: When does the POH say to drain the gascolator quick drains?
a: Before the first flight of the day and after each refueling
d: Only at each 50-hour inspection, and only by an A&P mechanic
Only when you suspect water contamination in the tanks
After every engine shutdown, before the fuel has time to settle
why: Drain them before the first flight of the day and after refueling to check for contamination. The tank drains are checked the same way.

q: You keep finding water while draining a gascolator, even after a full minute of draining. What does the POH say?
a: Have a mechanic check the fuel system
d: Keep draining until at least a gallon is out
Fly anyway; the engine-driven pump will separate the water
Top off the tank and then drain it again
why: Drain until the contamination stops. If it is still there after a minute of draining, the POH says to have a mechanic check the fuel system.

q: Where are the Seneca I's crossfeed drains?
a: On the bottom of the fuselage, inboard of the right flap
d: On the bottom of each engine nacelle, by the gascolator
Under each wing, outboard of the engine nacelle
Inside the nose baggage compartment, under the floor
why: The two crossfeed drains are under the fuselage, inboard of the right flap. In the walk-around they are drained with the right-side drains.

q: One alternator is inoperative before departure. What does the POH say about taking off into IFR conditions?
a: It is not recommended to take off into IFR with a single alternator
d: It is allowed if the operating alternator stays below 50 amps
It is allowed if the battery has been fully charged first
It is allowed once the inoperative alternator switch is OFF
why: Section 6 says an IFR takeoff on a single alternator is not recommended. With only one, another failure leaves the battery as the only source, and the POH wants each alternator held to 50 A in flight so the battery keeps charging.

q: Both alternators fail in flight. Per the POH, what determines how long the battery can carry the needed equipment?
a: The equipment's current draw, how soon you noticed, and battery condition
d: The equipment's current draw, engine RPM, and outside air temperature
Battery condition, engine RPM, and the alternator switch positions
Only the battery's 35 amp-hour rating, regardless of the load
why: With both alternators out, the battery is the only source, so turn off all unnecessary equipment. That's why the POH wants the ammeters and warning lights watched closely at night and in instrument flight.

q: With PROP DE-ICE switched on, how do you confirm the propeller deicers are drawing normal current?
a: The PROP DE-ICER ammeter needle is within its shaded band
d: A green PROP HEAT light comes on above the control quadrant
The WING-TAIL DE-ICER light flashes each time the timer cycles
The suction gauge dips briefly each time the timer cycles
why: Prop deice power goes through its own PROP DE-ICER ammeter to the timer, and a reading in the shaded portion is normal. On the ground you can also feel the pads warm in sequence.
